title: Lowest Common Ancestor
tagline: The deepest node that is an ancestor of both targets — via recursion or binary lifting.

complexity.time: O(n) one-shot, O(log n) with lifting

intuition.analogy: Two people trace their family trees upward. The first shared ancestor where their lines merge is the lowest common ancestor — the most recent relative they both descend from.
paragraphs: The LCA of two nodes is the deepest node that has both as descendants. For a single query, a clean recursion suffices: a node is the LCA if its left and right subtrees each contain one of the targets (or it is one of the targets).

When you must answer many LCA queries, precomputation pays off. Binary lifting stores, for each node, its 2^k-th ancestor. To find the LCA you first raise the deeper node to the same depth, then jump both up in powers of two until they're just below their common ancestor.
LCA underlies distance queries (dist(u,v) = depth[u] + depth[v] − 2·depth[lca]), path queries, and many competitive-programming tree problems.
intuition.keyIdea: Single query: recurse and merge where both targets appear. Many queries: precompute 2^k-th ancestors and jump.

steps.title: Recursive LCA (single query)
steps.detail: lca(node): if node is null or equals p or q, return node. Recurse left and right. If both return non-null, node is the LCA; otherwise propagate the non-null side.

steps.title: Binary lifting setup
steps.detail: DFS to record depth and up[v][0] = parent. Fill up[v][k] = up[ up[v][k-1] ][k-1] for all k.

steps.title: Answer a query
steps.detail: Lift the deeper node to match depths, then lift both simultaneously by decreasing powers of two while their ancestors differ; the parent of the result is the LCA.

complexity.time: O(n) per recursive query; O(n log n) preprocessing + O(log n) per lifted query
complexity.timeReason: Recursion touches each node once; binary lifting answers each query in log n jumps.
complexity.spaceReason: The ancestor table stores log n ancestors per node.

pitfalls: Recursive LCA assumes both nodes exist in the tree.
Binary lifting needs the depth equalisation step before the simultaneous jumps.
Off-by-one in the powers-of-two loop is the most common bug — iterate k from high to low.

dryRun.clickMoment: The LCA is the unique node where the searches for p and q come back from different sides. Above it, only one side is ever non-null.

problems.title: LCA of a Binary Tree
problems.statement: Find the LCA of two nodes in a binary tree.

approach: Recurse from the root. If the current node is null or equals p or q, return it.
Recurse left and right: if both sides return non-null, the current node is the split point (the LCA); otherwise propagate the single non-null side upward.

problems.title: LCA of a BST
problems.statement: Find the LCA in a binary search tree.
problems.hint: Walk down: go left if both < node, right if both > node, else you're at the LCA.

approach: In a BST the LCA is the first node where p and q split. Walk down from the root.
If both values are smaller go left, if both larger go right; otherwise the current node sits between them and is the LCA.

problems.title: LCA III (with parent pointers)
problems.statement: Find LCA when nodes have parent pointers.
problems.hint: Two-pointer technique like finding the intersection of two linked lists.

approach: With parent pointers, the LCA is the first common node on the two upward chains — exactly the linked-list intersection trick.
Two pointers walk up; when one hits the root, redirect it to the other node. They meet at the LCA after at most depth(p)+depth(q) steps.

problems.title: Distance Between Tree Nodes
problems.statement: Find the number of edges between two nodes.

approach: Distance(p, q) = depth(p) + depth(q) - 2·depth(lca), measuring edges through their lowest common ancestor.
Find the LCA, then the distance from it to each node by a short search. Equivalent to summing the two downward path lengths.

problems.title: Kth Ancestor of a Tree Node
problems.statement: Answer queries for the k-th ancestor of a node.
problems.hint: Binary lifting: decompose k into powers of two.

approach: Binary lifting precomputes up[j][v] = the 2^j-th ancestor of v. Any kth ancestor is reached by jumping the set bits of k.
Building the table is O(n log n); each query decomposes k into powers of two for O(log k).

complexity.time: O(n log n) build, O(log k) query
